recall.minute: Lexical semantics distinguishes lemmas from senses (polysemy: mouse) and relations: synonymy (couch/sofa, imperfect: big/large sister), similarity (coffee/tea), relatedness (coffee/cup, doctor/scalpel), antonymy, hypernymy (animal > dog > poodle) and meronymy (wheel/car); connotation adds affect (cheap vs inexpensive; valence, arousal, dominance). The distributional hypothesis (Firth: know a word by its company; ongchoi example) underlies vector semantics. Term-document matrices (battle [1, 0, 7, 13]) and term-term matrices (cherry near pie/sugar, digital near computer/data) give long sparse vectors. The dot product favours frequent words; cosine normalises it (digital/information 0.996, cherry/information 0.019). TF-IDF uses tf = log₁₀(count + 1) ('the' ×1000 → 3.0, 'data' ×10 → 1.04) and idf = log₁₀(N/df) (N = 100: df 5 → 1.30, df 100 → 0); PMI weights word-word counts. Dense 50–300-dimensional embeddings are learned by self-supervised prediction of neighbours; one-hot × embedding matrix selects a row (lookup trick).
